**Ionisation methods – a quick guide** | Field | Typical ionisation technique | Key advantages | Typical limitations | |-------|------------------------------|----------------|---------------------| | **Mass spectrometry (MS)** | **Electrospray ionisation (ESI)** | • Soft, preserves non‑covalent complexes
• Works with polar, high‑molecular‑weight analytes (proteins, peptides, nucleic acids)
• Easy coupling to LC | • Requires aqueous or polar solvents
• Poor for very non‑polar compounds | | | **Matrix‑assisted laser desorption/ionisation (MALDI)** | • Handles large biomolecules (proteins, polymers)
• Fast, high‑throughput
• Minimal sample prep | • Matrix interference in low‑mass region
• Less suitable for very polar analytes | | | **Atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI)** | • Good for moderately polar, low‑molecular‑weight compounds
• Compatible with LC‑MS | • Less effective for highly polar or large molecules | | | **Atmospheric pressure photoionisation (APPI)** | • Excellent for non‑polar, aromatic compounds
• Works with LC‑MS | • Requires UV lamp; limited to certain analytes | | | **Chemical ionisation (CI)** | • Soft ionisation, useful for structural elucidation | • Requires a reagent gas; less common in modern LC‑MS | | | **Electron ionisation (EI)** | • Standard for GC‑MS; provides reproducible fragmentation patterns | • Hard ionisation; not suitable for thermally labile or large molecules | | | **Field ionisation (FI)** | • Very soft; useful for large biomolecules | • Requires high vacuum and specialized equipment | | | **Laser desorption/ionisation (LDI)** | • No matrix needed; good for inorganic/organic mixtures | • Lower sensitivity compared to MALDI | | **Atomic/ionic physics** | **Photoionisation** | • Non‑contact, can be tuned to specific energies | • Requires UV/soft X‑ray sources | | | **Electron impact ionisation** | • Simple, widely used in electron spectroscopy | • Can fragment fragile species | | | **Field ionisation / field desorption** | • Very gentle; preserves molecular ions | • Requires high electric fields and vacuum | | | **Cold‑trap ionisation** | • Reduces fragmentation; useful for high‑resolution MS | • Complex instrumentation | --- ### Choosing the “best” method 1. **What you’re analysing** * **Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides, DNA)** → ESI or MALDI (ESI for LC‑MS, MALDI for MALDI‑TOF). * **Small, volatile, non‑polar molecules** → EI (GC‑MS) or APCI (LC‑MS). * **Non‑polar, aromatic compounds** → APPI or FI. * **Thermally labile or highly polar compounds** → ESI or APPI. 2. **Desired information** * **Structural elucidation** → EI or CI (GC‑MS) for detailed fragmentation. * **Quantitation of intact molecules** → ESI or MALDI (especially MALDI‑TOF for high‑throughput). * **Complex mixtures** → LC‑MS with ESI/APCI/APPI depending on polarity. 3. **Instrument constraints** * **Availability of a laser** → MALDI or LDI. * **Need for high‑resolution mass** → ESI coupled to Orbitrap or FT‑ICR. * **Speed** → MALDI (rapid spot‑to‑spot) or APCI (fast LC‑MS). 4. **Sample preparation** * **Minimal prep** → MALDI (matrix addition only). * **Solvent‑based prep** → ESI (solvent flow). --- ### Quick decision tree ``` ┌─ Is the analyte a large biomolecule? ──► Yes → ESI (LC‑MS) or MALDI (TOF) │ ├─ Is it small, volatile, non‑polar? ──► Yes → EI (GC‑MS) or APCI (LC‑MS) │ ├─ Is it non‑polar, aromatic? ──► Yes → APPI (LC‑MS) │ └─ Otherwise → ESI (LC‑MS) or APPI (if polar) ``` --- #### Bottom line There isn’t a single “best” ionisation method; the optimal choice depends on: * **Molecular size & polarity** * **Desired analytical outcome (qualitative vs. quantitative)** * **Instrument availability & operational constraints** For most modern LC‑MS workflows, **electrospray ionisation (ESI)** is the workhorse because of its softness, versatility, and compatibility with a wide range of analytes. For high‑throughput protein analysis, **MALDI‑TOF** is often preferred. If you’re dealing with non‑polar, aromatic compounds, **APPI** can outperform ESI/APCI. And for volatile, small molecules, **EI** remains the gold standard in GC‑MS. Feel free to let me know your specific application (e.g., proteomics, metabolomics, environmental analysis, etc.) and I can tailor the recommendation further!
